title: Nested loop, hash join and merge join, and why the planner picks one

videos.script: Two tables, one question: which customers bought what. Somewhere inside the server, rows from one table have to meet rows from the other. {{meet}} PostgreSQL has three ways to make them meet. {{three}} The nested loop takes each row on one side and looks up its partners on the other. It is perfect for ten rows and ruinous for a million. {{loop}} The hash join reads the smaller side into memory, as a hash table, and then streams the larger side past it once. It is the workhorse of reports. {{hash}} The merge join needs both sides sorted on the join key, and walks them together like two lists being merged. When the order comes free, from an index, it can be the cheapest of all. {{merge}} In this lesson you join the market's tables for real and read each method in its plan. You watch a hash spill to disk when its memory runs out. {{spill}} And you catch the planner choosing the slower of two joins, by eight times, and find which of its inputs led it there. {{wrong}} The method is never chosen at random. It follows from how many rows the planner expects on each side. Get that number wrong, and the join is wrong with it. {{estimate}}
